strengths: Well-motivated and novel idea: using traversal orders of uniform spanning trees over the image lattice provides a principled middle ground between fixed raster-scan order (locality/center-bias prior but no flexibility) and random permutation (flexibility but loss of locality/prior structure).

Solid theoretical grounding: the paper connects the method to graph theory (uniform spanning trees, Wilson's algorithm for efficient sampling, BFS vs. DFS tie-breaking analysis), and provides an explicit rejection-sampling algorithm (Algorithm 1) with a proof-sketch style justification (depth condition, Eq. 3) for postfix completion during editing.

Empirical motivation is supported by data: prediction-entropy analyses (Fig. 3, 4, and Appendix Fig. A) under random permutation training show token difficulty correlates with center bias/locality, substantiating the design choice to prioritize spanning-tree structured orders.

Strong quantitative results across four model scales (STAR-B/L/XL/XXL) on ImageNet-1k 256x256 class-conditional generation, matching or outperforming comparable-size SOTA discrete AR baselines (RAR, VAR, LlamaGen, RandAR) with minimal architectural change (only additive positional embeddings for the next-token position).

Convincing inpainting/postfix-completion evaluation across a range of masking ratios (0.1-0.9), with both quantitative (FID/IS/Precision/Recall) and qualitative comparisons showing STAR clearly outperforms the raster-scan RAR baseline for editing, which is a task conventional unidirectional AR models handle poorly.

Thorough ablation studies (Table 2 on order randomization strategy across training/inference stages, Table 3 on BFS vs. DFS and root-selection strategies for rejection-sampling efficiency) that isolate the contribution of the spanning-tree structure versus pure randomization/order annealing.

Reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, masking strategy pseudocode, and extended qualitative samples are provided in the supplementary material; changes to the base Decoder-only Causal AR Transformer are minimal and clearly described.
weaknesses: Experiments are limited to a single dataset/resolution (ImageNet-1k, 256x256, class-conditional generation); there is no demonstration on text-to-image, higher-resolution, or more diverse/naturalistic editing benchmarks, which limits evidence of broader impact and generalizability of the claimed prior-knowledge benefits.

The inpainting comparison is restricted essentially to RAR; other relevant bidirectional or randomized-order baselines shown in Table 1 (e.g., MAR, RandAR, VAR, or mask-based generative models like MaskGIT) are not evaluated on the editing task, so the claimed superiority for image editing is only demonstrated against one competitor.

No analysis of the computational/inference-time overhead introduced by the rejection-sampling procedure for postfix completion (Algorithm 1), despite Table 3 showing the number of trials needed can be substantial at certain masking ratios (e.g., ~60 trials at 0.1 ratio with random root); this could matter for practical deployment.

The gains in class-conditional generation quality over comparable-size raster-scan/randomized AR baselines (e.g., STAR-XXL vs RAR-XXL) are relatively incremental rather than dramatic, so the primary practical contribution is arguably the editing capability rather than raw generation quality.

Limited discussion of failure cases, limitations, or scenarios where the spanning-tree order might underperform (e.g., very large masks, non-connected/partial masks, or editing operations beyond inpainting such as outpainting or semantic edits), and no societal-impact discussion.

Some technical figures (e.g., Fig. 3/4 and Appendix Fig. A) are dense and would benefit from clearer exposition of their practical implications for readers less familiar with spanning-tree/entropy analysis.

strengths: Well-motivated and elegant idea: restricting the search space from the full N! permutations to the exp(N) space of uniform spanning trees on a lattice, structurally injecting prior knowledge (center bias, locality) into permutation AR modeling. The connection to well-known results on spanning tree counting/sampling (Wilson's algorithm) is nicely leveraged.

Strong empirical results: STAR matches or outperforms raster-scan AR (LlamaGen, RAR) and random-permutation AR (RandAR) baselines on ImageNet-1k class-conditional generation (FID/IS/P/R) while adding only minimal architectural overhead (only next-token position conditioning), and clearly outperforms other methods on native image inpainting without requiring token dropping/teacher forcing hacks used for DiT or RAR.

Thorough ablations and analysis: entropy analysis (Fig. 3, 8) linking spanning-tree traversal order to conditional model entropy patterns similar to raster-scan; center-bias quartile analysis; DFS vs BFS rejection-sampling trial/failure-rate comparison (Table 4) justifying design choices; sequence-order annealing ablation (Table 3); overhead quantification (<0.0004% of inference time).

The paper is generally clearly written, with a good high-level figure (Fig. 2) and an algorithmic description (Algorithm 1) of the rejection sampling procedure for postfix completion, aiding reproducibility. Hyperparameters and compute budgets (A100 GPU-days) are reported in the appendix.

The representation-learning experiment (Section 5, Fig. 9) is a nice additional piece of evidence that spanning-tree order also helps mitigate overfitting/improve linear-probe accuracy relative to raster-scan, suggesting the idea has value beyond generation quality alone.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to ImageNet-1k 256x256 class-conditional generation; no results on text-to-image or higher-resolution generation are provided, despite the paper's motivation citing multimodal/early-fusion models. This limits evidence for broader impact/generality of the claimed contribution.

The inpainting comparison (Table 2, Fig. 6-7) uses only masking ratios and random connected masks; there is no evaluation on realistic, application-driven editing tasks (e.g., object removal/insertion with semantically meaningful masks, editing benchmarks), so it's unclear how STAR performs in more practical image-editing use cases beyond synthetic random-mask inpainting.

The core method assumes the mask does not disconnect the graph and does not cover all lattice corners (Eq. 5-related constraint); violations require a multi-turn decomposition discussed only briefly in the appendix (Fig. A) without quantitative evaluation, leaving open how much this limitation affects real editing workflows.

Rejection sampling for spanning-tree construction, while shown to be cheap on average, could have heavier tails or failure modes for adversarial/complex mask shapes; Table 4 measures trials/failures only for random masks with ratios up to 0.9, not for structured or disconnected masks that are common in real editing (e.g., non-convex regions, multiple disjoint small holes).

Some choices (e.g., regular taxicab lattice as the sole graph structure, corner root selection, learnable positional embeddings vs. RoPE) are not deeply justified with alternative-design ablations beyond the DFS/BFS and root-selection comparisons; e.g., no ablation comparing to other structured sub-permutation spaces (e.g., Hilbert curve family, hierarchical/quad-tree orders) which would better substantiate that spanning trees are the best middle ground rather than just a reasonable one.

Comparisons in Table 1/2 involve models trained under possibly different compute/data budgets across baselines (parameter counts differ), and while FID gains are consistent, the improvements over RAR/RandAR at comparable model sizes are sometimes modest (e.g., STAR-XL FID 1.65 vs. RAR-XL FID 1.50 in Table 1), which is not explicitly acknowledged as a case where STAR underperforms in generation-only metrics despite superior inpainting.
